the rate of pecking is a function of the distance between a stimulus and a goal.

In summary, our research is concerned with
the effect of the stimulus properties of a discriminative stimulus on the rate at which a pigeon will peck at a key.
the effect of an added variable-interval stimulus upon the rate of response.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the rate of responding was a function of the size of the meter deflection.
the pigeon's behavior was determined by a function of the distance of the meter from the maximum deflection and the size of the step.
the pigeon was not responding to the meter deflections per se but to some other stimulus that was correlated with the deflection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the rate of responding was a function of the rate of movement of the voltmeters, not of the size of the meter deflection.
the rate of pecking on the first key increased as the probability of a deflection increased.
pigeons will peck at a key that is not associated with food if the pecks are followed by some other consequence.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the rate of pecking is not simply a function of the number of steps to a reinforcement, but is a function of the distance to a reinforcement, and this distance is not necessarily a simple linear function of the number to steps.
the rate of pecking on the first key (the “advance” key) is a function of the size of the meter deflection, and not the size of the reinforcement.
we found a very strong relationship between the size of the meter deflection and the rate of responding.
